To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the emergence of awareness can be explained by the pre-stimulus configuration of the EEG scalp potential field and that this pre-stimulus EEG activity is stronger in primary visual areas when awareness is absent.

(i) the differences in perceptually conscious and unconscious processing of weak visual stimuli at the threshold for awareness are reflected by different patterns of pre-stimuli activity in early visual areas, and (ii) these differences are reflected by the spatial configuration of scalp potential fields identified with multichannels EEG.
the emergence of awareness is linked to pre-stimulus EEG microstate maps that are different for targets that are correctly identified with and those correctly identified without awareness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the brain is able to predict the occurrence of a sensory stimulus.
the question of whether the differences in awareness for identical physical stimuli at the threshold for conscious perception can be explained by differences of pre-stimuli brain activity.
the question of whether the emergence of awareness can be explained by the activation of different brain networks at different stages of the perceptual process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EEG microstate maps are a good indicator for the state of the brain before the stimulus onset and that they are a good indicator of the awareness state after the stimulus onset.
the microstates of EEG are the most important factors for awareness and that the alpha power and phase are less important.
pre-stimulus brain states are not sufficient to explain awareness but are a necessary condition for it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the differences in awareness for the same physical stimuli are related to the pre-stimulus brain activity.
the emergence of perceptual consciousness is not just a function of stimulus processing, but it is also a function of global brain state.
pre-stimulus EEG microstate is a good predictor of the emergence of perceptual experience.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EEG microstate analysis is a promising tool to investigate the neural basis of conscious experience.
the global brain state preceding a stimulus onset can be used as a predictor of perceptual awareness, which can be measured by the EEG microstates and their generators in the primary visual cortex.

the differences in the pre-stimulus EEG microstate are associated with differences in awareness for identical stimuli, and that the differences in awareness can be explained by the differential pre-stimulust activation of primary visual area.
